deep.reconstruction:
Context (reconstructed from this page alone; the previous page is not available): f(x) is an irreducible equation over the base domain of rationality, of degree m = k·n. It is a 'Galois' (normal) equation: every root is a rational function of any one root r. A root ρ of an auxiliary equation is adjoined. Over the extended domain, f splits into k irreducible factors f(x,ρ), f(x,ρ_1), ..., f(x,ρ_{k-1}), each of degree n. Here ρ_1, ..., ρ_{k-1} are the conjugates of ρ singled out on earlier pages, and φ(ξ,r) is a function, rational in r over the base field, that expresses how the auxiliary quantity ξ (=ρ) depends on the root r.

Step 1. The page opens 'und folglich auch' (and consequently also): f(x,ρ) f(x,ρ_1) ··· f(x,ρ_{k-1}) = f(x). This is the factorization of f into the k conjugate factors. It presumably follows from the previous page: f is divisible by f(x,ρ), hence by each conjugate factor; these are distinct and irreducible, and the degrees add up.

Step 2. Let r, r', ..., r^{(n-1)} be the roots of f(x,ρ). Because f is normal, one may write r^{(i)} = θ^{(i)}(r), where the θ^{(i)} are rational functions with coefficients in the base domain. (Dedekind writes θ'r for θ'(r).)

Step 3. Claim: r_1, θ'(r_1), ..., θ^{(n-1)}(r_1) are again n mutually distinct roots of f(x)=0.
- Justification (mine, standard): f(θ^{(i)}(r)) = 0 is a rational relation satisfied by the root r of the irreducible f, so it holds for every root, in particular for r_1.
- If θ^{(i)}(r_1) = θ^{(j)}(r_1), the same transfer principle (from r_1 back to r) would give θ^{(i)}(r) = θ^{(j)}(r), which is impossible.

Step 4. The relations φ(ξ,r) = φ(ξ,θ'r) = ... = φ(ξ,θ^{(n-1)}r) hold as rational identities in the root r. Hence they hold with r replaced by r_1: φ(ξ,r_1) = φ(ξ,θ'r_1) = ... = φ(ξ,θ^{(n-1)}r_1). These relations express that all the θ^{(i)}r_1 attach to the same auxiliary root ρ_1 as r_1 does. Consequently the roots of f(x,ρ_1) may be taken as r_1^{(i)} = θ^{(i)}(r_1). Likewise for the factors belonging to ρ_2, ..., ρ_{k-1}.

Step 5. Conclusion: for each j = 0, ..., k-1,
 f(x,ρ_j) = f(x,ρ_j') = ... = f(x,ρ_j^{(ν-1)}) = ∏_{i=0}^{n-1} (x − θ^{(i)}(r_j)).
Here ρ_j, ρ_j', ..., ρ_j^{(ν-1)} are the ν conjugates of the auxiliary root that yield the same factor. So the k·ν roots of the auxiliary equation fall into k classes of ν, each class determining one factor.

In modern terms: the conjugate factors are obtained from one another by applying the same set of substitutions θ^{(i)} (the subgroup H = Gal(L/K(ρ)) acting on roots) to different starting roots r_j. The roots of f are thereby partitioned into the k cosets (orbits) r_j·H.

This serves Dedekind's development of Galois's theorem on the reduction of the group by adjunction of the roots of an auxiliary equation (Galois, Prop. II/III), within his early Galois-theory notes (c. 1855–58).

results.what: Factorization of the irreducible normal f into k conjugate factors over K(ρ), each with roots θ^{(i)}(r_j) obtained by the same rational substitutions from different starting roots
results.modern_name: Decomposition of the roots of a normal polynomial into orbits/cosets of the subgroup Gal(L/K(ρ)); conjugate factors over an intermediate field
results.usually_credited_to: Galois (1831, Mémoire, Props. II–III); systematized by Jordan (1870) and Dedekind's own lectures

results.what: Transfer of rational relations from one root to another root of an irreducible equation
results.modern_name: Conjugation principle / Abel–Galois irreducibility lemma (field isomorphism K(r) ≅ K(r_1))

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard exposition of Galois's adjunction theorem in Dedekind's well-known early Galois-theory notes (Göttingen lectures 1856–58, partly edited by Scharlau). The material is classical and Dedekind's engagement with it is documented.

checkable.asserts: Example of f(x,ρ)f(x,ρ_1)=f(x) with k=2, n=2, ρ=±sqrt(5), for the normal irreducible f = 5th cyclotomic polynomial
The factor x^2+(1-sqrt5)/2 x+1 has roots r and θ'(r)=r^4, a rational function of r
The same substitution θ'(x)=x^4 applied to another root r_1 gives the roots of the conjugate factor
